charts.title: Gross Profit, Operating Income & Net Income

sections.title: Rail Operating Metrics
sections.subtitle: Industry-specific efficiency, volume and yield metrics not derivable from the income statement

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Canadian National Railway Company: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Canadian National Railway Company: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Canadian National Railway Company: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

operatingRatio.title: Operating ratio
operatingRatio.content:
Operating ratio is operating expense divided by revenue -- the primary efficiency yardstick the whole rail industry is judged on. Lower is better: more of every revenue dollar falls to operating profit.

For Canadian National Railway Company: CN runs in the high-50s to low-60s%, among the best in North American rail (a 1-point move is roughly $170m of annual operating income at current revenue). Adjusted operating ratio strips out items management calls non-recurring (e.g. restructuring, legal charges), so compare both -- a persistent gap between the two is a flag that "adjustments" are becoming routine.

What to watch:

  • Direction over several years, not one quarter (ratio is noisy quarter to quarter on volume and weather)
  • Gap between reported and adjusted ratio widening
  • Peer railroads' ratios for relative positioning

railVolume.title: Rail volume metrics
railVolume.content:
Carloads is the count of rail cars moved. Gross ton-miles (GTM) is total weight (including the train itself) moved one mile; revenue ton-miles (RTM) is the weight of revenue-generating freight only, moved one mile -- the standard rail-industry traffic measure.

For Canadian National Railway Company: these are physical volume, not dollar figures -- they isolate whether revenue growth is coming from moving more freight or from pricing (compare against the Revenue chart above).

What to watch:

  • RTM growth diverging from revenue growth (a pricing/mix signal)
  • Carload trends by commodity group in the filings (grain, intermodal, petroleum) -- the blended total can mask a weak segment

freightYield.title: Freight revenue per RTM
freightYield.content:
Freight revenue per revenue ton-mile is the yield metric: how much revenue CN earns per unit of freight traffic moved. It rises with price increases, fuel surcharges and a richer traffic mix, and falls with discounting or a shift toward lower-rated bulk commodities.

For Canadian National Railway Company: read it alongside the Operating Ratio chart -- yield growth that outpaces cost inflation is what drives the operating ratio down over time.

What to watch:

  • Yield growth versus rail cost inflation (fuel, labour)
  • Mix shift between intermodal (lower yield, higher volume) and bulk/petroleum (higher yield)

headcount.title: Employees (end of period)
headcount.content:
Employees at period end is headcount, a labour-productivity input for a business where crew and terminal staff are among the largest controllable cost lines.

For Canadian National Railway Company: read against RTM growth above -- RTM growing faster than headcount is the labour-productivity gain behind operating-ratio improvement.

What to watch:

  • Headcount growth versus traffic (RTM) growth
  • Seasonal hiring/furloughs around peak grain and intermodal seasons

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Canadian National Railway Company: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Canadian National Railway Company: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Canadian National Railway Company: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Canadian National Railway Company: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Canadian National Railway Company: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Canadian National Railway Company: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Canadian National Railway Company: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
